expectations_used.clarify: Establishes how duplicate values and reused indices behave in findPairs before designing.
expectations_used.approach: States the algorithm and its complexity — e.g. a hashmap pass making it O(n) versus the naive O(n^2) — BEFORE writing code.
expectations_used.communicate: Talks through the pair-collection logic while implementing it.
expectations_used.implement: Implementation follows the stated algorithm for collecting unique index pairs.
expectations_used.verify: Dry-runs findPairs on an example with duplicates and re-runs the suite including the large-input test.
expectations_used.reflect: Restates the complexity and where the hashmap approach would break.

summary: Candidate started with a brute-force nested loop, confirmed the pairing/dedup contract by checking the test file, then diagnosed the large-input timeout as O(n^2) and rewrote to a hashmap-based O(n) solution. They dry-ran the new algorithm on a duplicate-containing example before saving, hit one failing edge case (complement equal to current value), fixed the insertion order, and verified all tests passed.

dimensions.analysis: After writing the initial brute-force loop, the candidate paused to resolve exactly the ambiguity the problem calls out — whether pairs or indices needed deduping, and how duplicate values interact with index reuse — by reading the test file rather than guessing. They then explicitly reconciled this with their existing implementation.

The first pass was only a vague 'brute force first' intent, but once the timing failure surfaced, the candidate explicitly named the mechanism (nested loop is O(n^2) over ~10k elements) and stated the replacement algorithm and its complexity (hashmap of value-to-indices, O(n) single pass) before writing any code.

The candidate narrated almost every step: the initial loop logic, the complexity diagnosis, the hashmap design, and a full manual dry run with concrete values, giving a transcript that fully explains the path taken.

Edits tracked the stated plans in order: brute force first, then a full rewrite to the hashmap approach, then a targeted fix for the complement-equals-self edge case discovered during testing, with no unexplained scope changes.

Before trusting the hashmap rewrite, the candidate manually traced it against a duplicate-containing example, then ran the full suite, and after a failure diagnosed and fixed the bug before re-running to confirm a full green pass including the large-input test.

The candidate correctly identified the root cause of the failing edge case (checking the map before inserting the current value, not after) and closed with a correct restatement of the algorithm's time and space complexity, tying the fix to the underlying mechanism rather than just citing green tests.
